alcohol-units-and-low-risk-drinking.name: Alcohol units: the UK low-risk drinking advice
alcohol-units-and-low-risk-drinking.summary: The UK Chief Medical Officers advise adults not to regularly drink more than 14 units a week, spread over three days or more.
keyPoints: The UK Chief Medical Officers advise that adults should not regularly drink more than 14 units of alcohol a week.
The guidance says there is no completely safe level of regular drinking; 14 units a week is described as a low-risk level, not a safe one.
One unit is 10 millilitres, or 8 grams, of pure alcohol, and the strength printed on a label as ABV can be used to work out units.
For anyone who is pregnant or could become pregnant, the Chief Medical Officers advise that the safest approach is not to drink alcohol at all.

body.heading: What is the UK low-risk drinking advice?
body.body: The UK Chief Medical Officers advise that, to keep the risk of harm from alcohol low, adults should not regularly drink more than 14 units a week. For someone who drinks as much as 14 units, the advice is to spread it evenly over three days or more. The guidance also says there is no completely safe level of regular drinking, so 14 units is a way to keep risk low rather than a safe amount. Some older leaflets still quote daily limits, but the weekly figure is the one in the current guidance.

body.heading: What is an alcohol unit?
body.body: One unit is 10 millilitres of pure alcohol, which is 8 grams. The strength of a drink is shown on the label as alcohol by volume, or ABV. Units can be worked out by multiplying the volume in millilitres by the ABV percentage and dividing by 1,000. Using that method, a pint of strong lager at 5.2% ABV comes to about three units. As a guide, 14 units is about six pints of average-strength beer or six medium glasses of average-strength wine.

body.heading: What does drinking above the guidance do to health?
body.body: The Chief Medical Officers' guidance says regular drinking above the low-risk level raises the risk of dying from long-term illnesses and from accidents and injuries, and alcohol is a risk factor for seven types of cancer. The guidance also names accidents and injuries among the short-term risks of heavy drinking. Drinking a large amount in a short time carries a particular risk of alcohol poisoning. Mouth cancers are more common among people who drink, and the risk is higher still when drinking is combined with smoking or any form of tobacco.

body.heading: Does keeping to 14 units remove the risk?
body.body: The 2016 review behind the guidance estimated that the lifetime risk of dying from an alcohol-related condition is around 1 per cent, or a little under, for people drinking at the low-risk level. Heavier drinking raises the risk further. The guidance is therefore described as a way to keep risk low, not to remove it.

body.heading: Who is advised not to drink at all?
body.body: For anyone who is pregnant or thinks they could become pregnant, the Chief Medical Officers advise that the safest approach is not to drink alcohol at all.

body.heading: When might someone need support with drinking?
body.body: Signs listed as a reason to seek support include drinking more over time, struggling to cut down, poor sleep, thinking ahead to the next drink, risky behaviour and concern from other people.

body.heading: How does the NHS suggest cutting down?
body.body: The NHS Better Health site points people to their local alcohol support service, or to Drinkline on 0300 123 1110, which it describes as free, confidential help for anyone concerned about their own or someone else's drinking. It also offers the NHS Drink Free Days app for setting a weekly unit target. NHS pages describe a drinks diary as a way to see how much is being drunk, in which situations, and how cutting down could start. Having several alcohol-free days each week is another suggestion, as are choosing lower-strength drinks and alternating alcoholic drinks with soft drinks.

body.heading: What treatment exists for alcohol dependence?
body.body: The NHS says treatment for alcohol use disorder is available from a GP or a specialist alcohol service. Options it lists include counselling, self-help groups, talking therapies such as CBT, and medicines. Alcoholics Anonymous and SMART Recovery are named as self-help groups, and Al-Anon Family Groups as support for families and friends of people who drink. The NHS says a person who is not ready to stop, or who only wants to cut down, will be supported to reduce drinking to a safer level. The NHS says it can be very dangerous to stop drinking suddenly for someone who is dependent on alcohol, and that anyone who gets withdrawal symptoms should get medical help before trying to stop; for severe symptoms such as confusion, hallucinations or a seizure it advises calling 999 or going to A&E.

blood-pressure-at-home-how-it-works.name: Home blood pressure checks: how they work
blood-pressure-at-home-how-it-works.summary: The NHS says blood pressure can be checked at home with a monitor, with the cuff on the upper arm and the person sitting with their back supported; local NHS leaflets also advise avoiding caffeine and smoking beforehand.
keyPoints: High blood pressure does not usually cause symptoms, so measuring it is the way to find out.
Blood pressure is written as two numbers, the first higher than the second.
NHS-linked guidance recommends an upper arm monitor rather than a wrist or finger device.
A GP or nurse advises how often to check blood pressure at home.

body.heading: What does a blood pressure check show?
body.body: The NHS says a blood pressure test can check whether blood pressure is too high or too low. High blood pressure does not usually have any symptoms. Readings are given as two numbers, for example 140/90, measured in millimetres of mercury (mmHg).

body.heading: Can people check at home?
body.body: The NHS says blood pressure can also be checked at home with a monitor. NHS England has a programme of home blood pressure monitoring through GP practices. The NHS says blood pressure is usually considered high at a lower figure when checked at home than when checked by a healthcare professional.

body.heading: How is a home reading usually taken?
body.body: Local NHS guides recommend an upper arm monitor with a cuff that fits snugly, and say that wrist devices are not recommended. Guides describe sitting quietly for about five minutes with feet flat and the back supported, and avoiding caffeine, smoking and exercise for about 30 minutes beforehand. Guides often suggest taking readings twice in the morning and twice in the evening for about a week, with the average worked out afterwards, although the number of readings differs between guides. Guides advise leaving about a minute between two readings, and the GP or nurse advises on timing around medicines because guides differ. One guide recommends choosing a monitor validated by the British and Irish Hypertension Society.

body.heading: What happens next?
body.body: One NHS integrated care board page says the GP or nurse advises how often to check. Blood Pressure UK advises re-checking after resting for five minutes if a reading is still high. The NHS advises calling 999 for possible heart attack symptoms such as chest pain with sweating or breathlessness, and contacting NHS 111 about frequent headaches, blurred vision or chest pain that comes and goes; the British Heart Foundation advises contacting a GP about symptoms that could be caused by high blood pressure.

bone-health-keeping-bones-strong.name: Bone health: what helps keep bones strong
bone-health-keeping-bones-strong.summary: NHS pages link bone health to weight-bearing exercise, calcium, vitamin D, not smoking and keeping alcohol low.
keyPoints: NHS guidance describes weight-bearing and resistance exercise as particularly important for bone strength.
Calcium is important for bone health, and vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium.
Being inactive, having a low body weight, smoking and heavy drinking are listed as risk factors for weaker bones.
The NHS advises adults aged 65 and over to include strength and balance activities on at least two days a week.

body.heading: What helps keep bones strong?
body.body: NHS guidance describes weight-bearing and resistance exercise as particularly important for improving bone density. Running, skipping, dancing, aerobics and jumping are named as higher-impact examples that strengthen muscles, ligaments and joints. Swimming and cycling support general fitness but are not weight-bearing, so they do less for the bones. Lack of physical activity is listed as a risk factor for osteoporosis.

body.heading: What do calcium and vitamin D do?
body.body: The NHS says most adults should be able to get the calcium they need from their daily diet. Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium, and the NHS says it can be difficult to get enough vitamin D from food alone, so a daily supplement may be considered. Sunlight from about late March or early April to the end of September helps the body make vitamin D, and the NHS suggests considering a daily vitamin D supplement.

body.heading: What raises the risk of weaker bones?
body.body: Osteopenia is the stage of bone loss before osteoporosis, and being underweight is listed among the risk factors for bone loss. Smoking and heavy drinking are also listed, and one source gives the low-risk alcohol guidance of less than 14 units a week. The Royal Osteoporosis Society says too much salt may increase the amount of calcium lost in urine.

body.heading: What changes after 65?
body.body: NHS guidance for people aged 65 and over advises activities that improve strength, balance and flexibility on at least two days a week. It also advises 150 minutes (2 and a half hours) of moderate-intensity activity a week, ideally spread across the days. NHS 111 Wales suggests that people diagnosed with osteoporosis talk to a GP or health specialist before starting a new exercise programme. A DEXA bone density scan is often used to help diagnose osteoporosis or to assess the risk of it.

cholesterol-and-diet-what-the-nhs-says.name: High cholesterol: diet, tests and medicines
cholesterol-and-diet-what-the-nhs-says.summary: The NHS says cutting down on saturated fat can help lower cholesterol, and that medicines such as statins are considered when lifestyle changes are not enough.
keyPoints: High cholesterol means too much of a fatty substance called cholesterol in the blood, and it usually causes no symptoms.
The NHS advises cutting down on fatty food, especially saturated fat, and swapping to unsaturated fats.
Soluble fibre from foods such as oats, barley, beans and lentils is described as helping to lower cholesterol.
A blood test measures cholesterol, and an NHS Health Check in England may offer it.

body.heading: What is cholesterol and why does it matter?
body.body: High cholesterol means having too much of a fatty substance called cholesterol in the blood. Too much cholesterol in the blood can build up in the artery walls and make them narrower over time. HDL is often called good cholesterol because it helps clear excess cholesterol from the blood, while LDL is often called bad cholesterol because it can build up in artery walls. High cholesterol usually causes no symptoms, which is why a blood test is used to find it.

body.heading: Who is more likely to have it?
body.body: Causes and risk factors listed include eating a lot of food high in saturated fat and a family history of high cholesterol. It can also run in families, and the British Heart Foundation lists ethnicity, being male and having been through the menopause among the factors that raise risk.

body.heading: What does diet change?
body.body: The NHS advises cutting down on fatty food, especially food containing saturated fat. The NHS suggests unsaturated fats instead, such as oily fish, nuts, seeds and olive or rapeseed oil, and lists meat pies, butter, cakes and coconut or palm oil among foods to limit. Soluble fibre from oats, barley, beans, pulses and lentils is described as helping to lower cholesterol. Plant sterols and stanols, added to some foods such as spreads, can also help lower cholesterol. The British Heart Foundation says cholesterol in food has a minimal impact on blood cholesterol levels, and that cutting down on saturated fat matters more.

body.heading: When are medicines considered?
body.body: The NHS says medicine may be needed if cholesterol has not gone down after changes to diet and lifestyle, or if a person is at high risk of a heart attack or stroke. Statins are the most common medicine for high cholesterol, and the NHS says people usually need to take them for life.

body.heading: How is cholesterol tested?
body.body: Testing is a blood test. In England it can be offered as part of an NHS Health Check for people aged 40 to 74 who do not already have cardiovascular disease. A GP may also suggest a test for someone with high blood pressure, diabetes, overweight, smoking or a family history of heart disease. Targets depend on factors such as age and other health conditions, so a clinician advises what applies to each person.

eatwell-guide-healthy-eating.name: The Eatwell Guide: a balanced diet explained
eatwell-guide-healthy-eating.summary: The Eatwell Guide shows the proportions of food groups in a balanced UK diet, with fruit, vegetables and starchy foods making up just over a third each.
keyPoints: The NHS Eatwell Guide divides food into groups and shows how much of each makes up a balanced diet.
Fruit and vegetables and starchy foods each make up just over a third of the guide, with higher-fibre starchy choices preferred.
NHS advice is at least five portions of a variety of fruit and vegetables a day, and at least two portions of fish a week, one of them oily.
Foods high in fat, salt and sugar sit outside the main groups and are meant to be eaten less often and in small amounts.

body.heading: What is the Eatwell Guide?
body.body: The Eatwell Guide is the UK government's picture of a balanced diet, and the NHS explains it on its Live Well pages. It divides the foods people eat into groups and shows roughly what share of the diet each should make up. Foods and drinks high in fat, salt and sugar sit outside the main groups, and the guide says they should be eaten less often and in small amounts.

body.heading: How much fruit, vegetables and starchy food?
body.body: Fruit and vegetables make up just over a third of the food in the guide. The NHS advises at least five portions of a variety of fruit and vegetables a day. A portion of fresh, canned or frozen fruit or vegetables is 80 grams. Starchy foods also make up just over a third of the guide, and the NHS recommends choosing wholegrain or higher-fibre versions where possible.

body.heading: What about protein, dairy and oils?
body.body: The NHS lists beans, pulses, fish, eggs and meat among good sources of protein. The NHS advises at least two portions of fish a week, including at least one portion of oily fish. For dairy and alternatives the guide points to lower-fat and lower-sugar choices where possible. Unsaturated oils and spreads are the choice for oils, eaten in small amounts.

body.heading: What does the NHS say about fat, sugar and salt?
body.body: NHS healthy eating advice includes cutting down on saturated fat and sugar and eating less salt. Fruit juice and smoothies are limited to a total of 150 millilitres a day, because they are high in sugar. The NHS says sugary drinks can be swapped for diet, sugar-free or no-added-sugar versions.

body.heading: Where do drinks, breakfast and weight fit in?
body.body: The NHS tips say that a healthy, balanced diet can help maintain a healthy weight, and that regular exercise may help reduce the risk of serious health conditions. They describe a breakfast high in fibre and low in fat, sugar and salt as one way to be part of a balanced diet.

body.heading: How do salt and saturated fat fit in?
body.body: The NHS advises adults and children aged 11 and over to have no more than 6 grams of salt a day, and younger children less. The NHS says around three quarters of the salt people eat comes from packaged and everyday foods. Salt is linked to high blood pressure, which can lead to heart disease or stroke. Too much saturated fat can increase cholesterol in the blood and so the risk of heart disease, and the NHS suggests swapping towards unsaturated fats such as vegetable oils, oily fish and avocados.

body.heading: What do food labels show?
body.body: UK nutrition labels show energy, fat, saturates, carbohydrate, sugars, protein and salt. Front-of-pack labels use red, amber and green colours to show whether a food is high, medium or low in fat, saturated fat, sugars and salt. The NHS lists sweets, sugary drinks, cakes, biscuits, pastries and breakfast cereals among common sources of added sugar, and says the label and ingredients list can show how much sugar a food contains.

healthy-weight-bmi-explained.name: Healthy weight: what BMI shows and what it misses
healthy-weight-bmi-explained.summary: BMI is an NHS check on whether weight suits height, but it cannot tell muscle from fat, so waist size and a GP discussion add to it.
keyPoints: The NHS BMI calculator checks whether a person is a healthy weight for their height.
BMI cannot tell muscle from fat, so very muscular people may be rated overweight and people who lose muscle with age may still fall in the healthy range.
The NHS says Black, Asian and some other minority ethnic groups have a higher risk of some long-term conditions at a lower BMI.
NHS treatment for obesity ranges from lifestyle changes and weight management programmes to medicines and surgery.

body.heading: What does BMI measure?
body.body: Body mass index, or BMI, is calculated from height and weight, and the NHS calculator uses it to check whether an adult is a healthy weight for their height. The calculator shows which category a result falls in, and the NHS gives a different healthy range for Black, Asian and some other minority ethnic groups. The reason given is that these groups have a higher risk of developing some long-term conditions, such as type 2 diabetes, at a lower BMI.

body.heading: What are the limits of BMI?
body.body: BMI cannot tell the difference between muscle and fat. Very muscular people and athletes may be rated overweight or obese despite low body fat. Adults who lose muscle as they get older may fall in the healthy weight range even though they may be carrying excess fat.

body.heading: Why does waist size matter?
body.body: The NHS gives a method for measuring the waist: find the bottom of the ribs and the top of the hips, place a tape measure midway between them, and measure after breathing out naturally. The NHS and NICE describe a waist measurement of more than half a person's height as linked with increased health risks. The NHS advises seeing a GP for help with losing weight, or if the waist measurement is more than half of height.

body.heading: What treatment does the NHS offer?
body.body: The NHS says a GP can advise on weight loss and on options such as weight management programmes, medicines or surgery. Options include lifestyle changes, weight management programmes, medicines and surgery. Local NHS specialist weight management services, often called tier 3, usually have a team that can include a doctor, dietitians, specialist nurses and psychologists. NHS access to weight-loss injections such as semaglutide and tirzepatide depends on eligibility criteria and varies by area; some are offered through specialist weight management services, and tirzepatide is being introduced through GP practices in phases for people with the highest clinical need.

body.heading: What health risks are linked to excess weight?
body.body: The NHS lists type 2 diabetes, heart disease, stroke, high blood pressure, several cancers, osteoarthritis and fatty liver disease among conditions linked to excess weight.

body.heading: Why does weight change?
body.body: The NHS describes overweight and obesity as having more body fat than the body needs. It can happen when a person eats or drinks more than the body needs or does not do enough physical activity. Other factors listed include genes, some medicines, and some health conditions such as an underactive thyroid.

body.heading: What does a GP check, and what support is free?
body.body: The NHS says a GP looks for possible underlying causes of obesity, for example a medicine the person is taking. The NHS offers a free 12-week weight loss plan as an app. The NHS says that for someone living with obesity, losing about 3 per cent of starting body weight can reduce the risk of obesity-related complications.

physical-activity-guidelines-adults.name: How much exercise adults need each week
physical-activity-guidelines-adults.summary: The NHS says adults aged 19 to 64 should do at least 150 minutes of moderate activity or 75 minutes of vigorous activity a week, plus strength work.
keyPoints: The NHS lists at least 150 minutes of moderate activity or 75 minutes of vigorous activity a week for adults aged 19 to 64.
Strengthening activities for the major muscle groups on at least two days a week are in addition to the aerobic minutes.
The NHS talk test separates moderate activity, where a person can talk but not sing, from vigorous activity, where only a few words fit between breaths.
The guidance also advises reducing long periods of sitting, and the 2019 update dropped the older rule that activity must come in bouts of at least ten minutes.

body.heading: How much activity do adults aged 19 to 64 need?
body.body: The NHS says adults aged 19 to 64 should aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate intensity activity a week, or 75 minutes of vigorous intensity activity a week. It also describes a mix of moderate and vigorous activity as a way of reaching the target. The NHS adds that 75 minutes of vigorous activity a week can give similar health benefits to 150 minutes of moderate activity. The guidance says activity should be spread across the week, and that all adults should aim to be active every day.

body.heading: What counts as moderate or vigorous?
body.body: The NHS uses a talk test: at moderate intensity a person can still talk but not sing. Brisk walking, cycling, dancing, water aerobics and pushing a lawn mower are listed as moderate activities. At vigorous intensity breathing becomes hard and fast, and a person cannot say more than a few words without pausing for breath. Running, swimming, fast or uphill cycling, skipping and team sports are listed as vigorous activities. The UK Chief Medical Officers' guidelines say very vigorous activity, such as sprinting or stair climbing, can count too, in shorter periods or mixed with other intensities.

body.heading: What are strengthening activities?
body.body: The NHS says adults should do strengthening activities on at least two days a week, working all the major muscle groups: legs, hips, back, abdomen, chest, shoulders and arms. Lifting weights, push-ups, sit-ups, heavy gardening such as digging and carrying heavy shopping are given as examples, along with yoga, pilates and tai chi. The NHS says these sessions are needed in addition to the aerobic minutes, because they do not count toward the 150 minutes. The Chief Medical Officers' guidance adds that any strengthening activity is better than none.

body.heading: Does sitting still matter?
body.body: The NHS guidance advises reducing the time spent sitting or lying down, and breaking up long periods of not moving with some activity. The Chief Medical Officers' guidance says adults should aim to minimise time spent sitting and, where possible, break up long inactive periods with at least light activity.

body.heading: What do the guidelines say about benefits and short bouts?
body.body: The NHS says exercising even once or twice a week can reduce the risk of heart disease or stroke. The 2019 revision of the UK guidelines removed the earlier rule that activity must come in bouts of at least ten minutes. The guidance says there is no minimum amount of physical activity needed for some health benefit.

body.heading: What does regular activity do for health?
body.body: The NHS says regular activity lowers the risk of conditions including heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes, depression and dementia. It also says activity can improve self-esteem, mood, sleep quality and energy.

body.heading: What changes for adults aged 65 and over?
body.body: NHS guidance for older adults advises being active every day, even lightly. It recommends activities that improve strength, balance and flexibility on at least two days a week, and 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity a week. The NHS advises speaking to a GP first for anyone who has not exercised for some time or who has medical conditions or concerns.

sleep-problems-what-helps.name: Sleep problems: what helps and when to get help
sleep-problems-what-helps.summary: The NHS says insomnia usually improves by changing sleeping habits, and that a GP can arrange CBT when habits alone do not help.
keyPoints: The NHS describes insomnia as regular difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep or waking too early.
A steady bedtime and wake time, a dark, quiet room and winding down without screens are habits the NHS Every Mind Matters pages describe for better sleep.
The NHS suggests seeing a GP if changing habits has not helped, or if sleep trouble has lasted for months.
Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is the main treatment described by NHS sources; sleeping pills are rarely prescribed.

body.heading: What counts as insomnia?
body.body:
The NHS says a person who regularly finds it hard to fall asleep, stay asleep or wake up too early may have insomnia. It also says insomnia usually gets better by changing sleeping habits.

A primary care pathway from NHS South Yorkshire advises considering life events and physical or mental health problems as possible triggers of insomnia. Primary care guidance for GPs in the NHS lists physical conditions such as sleep apnoea among the possible causes of insomnia. It also suggests that a clinician asks whether a medicine could be a cause, and considers anxiety or depression as possible underlying factors.

body.heading: Which sleep habits do NHS pages describe?
body.body:
The NHS Every Mind Matters pages say a regular sleep routine can make it easier to fall asleep, because going to bed and getting up at similar times each day helps the body know when it is time to sleep. They suggest keeping the same routine on days off. They also suggest keeping phones, tablets and computers away for an hour before bed, because the light can delay sleep. Reading, meditation or breathing exercises are given as alternatives.

A dark, quiet and cool bedroom is a recurring recommendation across NHS pages. NHS pages also advise against caffeine, smoking and alcohol in the hours before bed, although the exact timing differs from page to page. Some pages advise against napping during the day and describe regular daytime exercise as helpful. For someone who worries in bed, the NHS suggests writing a list of tasks for the next day before going to sleep.

body.heading: What does the NHS suggest when sleep will not come?
body.body: If a person is still awake after about 20 minutes, the NHS suggests getting up, doing something relaxing in another room, and going back to bed when sleepy.

body.heading: When does the NHS suggest seeing a GP?
body.body: The NHS suggests seeing a GP if changing sleeping habits has not helped insomnia, or if there has been trouble sleeping for months. A GP may refer a person for cognitive behavioural therapy, or CBT, which helps change the thoughts and behaviours that get in the way of sleep. The NHS says GPs now rarely prescribe sleeping pills for insomnia, because they can have serious side effects and a person can become dependent on them.

body.heading: What does CBT for insomnia involve?
body.body: The NHS recommends cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, known as CBT-I, as the first treatment for insomnia. CBT-I can be delivered in person, in groups or online, for example through the Sleepio programme, which is designed to be completed over six weeks; availability and cost to the patient vary by area. A primary care guideline from Buckinghamshire, Oxfordshire and Berkshire West advises that medicines are best avoided in the long-term management of insomnia.

body.heading: How much sleep do adults need, and why does it matter?
body.body: NHS sources put the amount most adults need at about 7 to 9 hours a night. One NHS page says age, health and daily routine can all affect how much sleep a person needs. NHS Every Mind Matters says getting enough sleep can support mood, energy, the immune system and overall health. A United States guide from the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute adds that regularly getting too little or very poor quality sleep increases the risk of high blood pressure, heart disease and other health problems. NHS pages list feeling very tired, irritable or sleepy during the day among the signs of not sleeping enough.

body.heading: Could another sleep disorder be involved?
body.body: The NHS says a person may be referred to a sleep clinic if they have symptoms of another sleep disorder, such as sleep apnoea.

stop-smoking-nhs-support.name: Stopping smoking: the support the NHS offers
stop-smoking-nhs-support.summary: NHS stop smoking services offer nicotine replacement, medicines and professional support, and people in England can self-refer through NHS Better Health.
keyPoints: NHS stop smoking services provide nicotine replacement therapy and prescription medicines, together with professional support in the first months after quitting.
Vapes are not available as medicines on the NHS, though some local services may offer a free starter pack.
The NHS says cravings are short-lived and that withdrawal symptoms are temporary.

body.heading: What help do NHS stop smoking services provide?
body.body: NHS stop smoking services offer information and advice and professional support during the first few months after someone stops smoking. They provide nicotine replacement therapy, such as patches and gum, and medicines such as varenicline and bupropion. In England people can refer themselves to a local service through the NHS Better Health website, and can also speak to a GP. What a local service offers, such as eligibility for a free e-cigarette starter pack, varies by area.

body.heading: How do nicotine replacement and medicines work?
body.body: Nicotine replacement therapy comes as patches, gum, lozenges, microtabs, and mouth and nasal sprays. The NHS says nicotine replacement therapy gives the body nicotine without the other harmful chemicals found in cigarettes and tobacco. Varenicline works by blocking the effects of nicotine in the brain. NHS pages say that a nicotine-free medicine such as varenicline or cytisine can be combined with a nicotine product, and describe the combination as giving the best chance of success.

body.heading: Where do vapes fit in?
body.body: E-cigarettes are not currently available as medicines, so stop smoking services cannot supply them and they cannot be prescribed on the NHS. Some local stop smoking services may still offer a free starter pack.

body.heading: What happens in the body after stopping?
body.body: The NHS sets out a timeline: within about 20 minutes the pulse rate begins to return to normal. By 48 hours carbon monoxide levels in the blood have fallen to those of a non-smoker. After one year the risk of a heart attack is about half that of a person who smokes, and after ten years the risk of lung cancer is about half. NHS pages also report mental health benefits: once the withdrawal stage has passed, people report less anxiety, depression and stress.

body.heading: What are cravings and withdrawal like?
body.body: The NHS says withdrawal symptoms are temporary, usually strongest in the first week and lasting on average three to four weeks. NHS inform, the Scottish NHS site, says cravings should ease after the first two to three weeks. The NHS says an individual craving lasts only a short time. Walking, chewing sugar-free gum and deep breathing are among the coping ideas it lists.

body.heading: What other support is available?
body.body: In November 2024 NHS England announced a rollout of varenicline, a stop smoking pill, to help tens of thousands of people a year try to quit.

body.heading: Why does the NHS stress stopping?
body.body: The NHS Better Health site says the harm from smoking reaches beyond the lungs, including a higher risk of dementia and inflammation that can worsen joint pain. The relief a cigarette seems to give from stress is short-lived, and smoking can make anxiety and low mood worse over time, according to the NHS.

stress-symptoms-and-getting-help.name: Stress: how it shows up and where to get help
stress-symptoms-and-getting-help.summary: Stress is a reaction to mental or emotional pressure that can affect mood, body and behaviour, and the NHS says support is available when it affects daily life.
keyPoints: The NHS describes stress as usually a reaction to mental or emotional pressure, often linked to feeling a loss of control.
Stress can show up as emotional changes, physical symptoms such as headaches and stomach problems, and changes in behaviour.
The NHS says too much stress can affect mood, the body and relationships.
Adults in England can refer themselves to NHS Talking Therapies without seeing a GP.

body.heading: What is stress?
body.body: The NHS describes stress as usually a reaction to mental or emotional pressure, often related to feeling a loss of control over something, though sometimes there is no obvious cause. Common triggers it lists include pressure at work, relationship or family difficulties, money worries, illness and bereavement. The NHS says most people feel stressed sometimes and some find stress helpful or even motivating, but that if it is affecting life there are things that may help. The NHS says too much stress can affect mood, the body and relationships.

body.heading: How does stress show up in the body and behaviour?
body.body: The NHS says stress can affect emotions, causing feelings such as irritability, anger and tearfulness. Physical symptoms listed include headaches, stomach problems, muscle tension and dizziness. Behaviour can change too, for example with sleep problems, loss of appetite, or drinking or smoking more.

body.heading: What does the NHS suggest for managing stress?
body.body: NHS pages suggest identifying the cause as the first step, then breaking large tasks into small targets and focusing on what can be changed. Controlled breathing, deep muscle relaxation and mindful breathing are listed as ways to reduce tension and some of the physical signs of stress. Talking to trusted friends, family or colleagues, or contacting a helpline, is also suggested. The NHS advises against using alcohol, cigarettes, gambling or drugs to relieve stress, because these can contribute to poor mental health.

body.heading: When does the NHS suggest getting help?
body.body: If urgent help is needed for mental health but it is not an emergency, the NHS says to use NHS 111 online or call 111 and choose the mental health option, or to ask for an urgent GP appointment. In England, adults aged 18 and over can refer themselves directly to NHS Talking Therapies without seeing a GP, and in some areas the minimum age is 16. If stress has led to thoughts of self-harm or suicide, call 999 if there is immediate danger, use NHS 111 and choose the mental health option for urgent help, or contact Samaritans free at any time on 116 123.

body.heading: What happens in the body during stress?
body.body: An NHS self-help guide describes stress as the body's reaction to feeling under threat, known as the fight or flight response, and says a certain amount of pressure can be helpful and motivating. The British Heart Foundation explains that the brain signals the body to release hormones such as adrenaline and cortisol. It says that if this response keeps being switched on again and again, over time it can take its toll on the body.

vitamin-d-and-supplements-who-needs-them.name: Vitamins and supplements: who may need them
vitamin-d-and-supplements-who-needs-them.summary: The NHS says a varied and balanced diet should provide enough of several vitamins, but advises supplements for some people, including vitamin D in autumn and winter and folic acid in early pregnancy.
keyPoints: NHS pages advise that everyone should consider taking a vitamin D supplement in autumn and winter.
Some groups, including people who are rarely outdoors and people with dark skin, are advised to take vitamin D all year.
The NHS advises anyone who is pregnant or could become pregnant to take a folic acid supplement until the twelfth week of pregnancy.
More is not always better: the NHS warns that very high vitamin D intakes could be harmful.

body.heading: Can a balanced diet provide everything?
body.body: NHS pages say that a varied and balanced diet should provide all that is needed of some vitamins, such as vitamin A, while supplements are advised for some groups. The NHS says that from about late March or early April to the end of September, most people can make the vitamin D they need from sunlight on the skin.

body.heading: Who is advised to take vitamin D?
body.body: The NHS says everyone should consider a daily vitamin D supplement in autumn and winter. In England the NHS advises all babies and children aged 1 to 4 to take vitamin D throughout the year, and NHS inform in Scotland describes babies and children under 5 as a higher-risk group. Some groups are advised to take it all year: people who are not often outdoors, such as those who are frail or housebound or living in care homes, people who usually cover most of their skin outdoors, and people with dark skin from African, African-Caribbean or South Asian backgrounds. For breastfed babies the NHS advises a daily vitamin D supplement throughout the year, and children aged 1 to 4 are also advised to take it year-round. Healthy Start vitamin products are free for eligible families.

body.heading: What does the NHS say about pregnancy?
body.body: Anyone who is pregnant or could become pregnant is advised to take a daily folic acid supplement until the twelfth week of pregnancy. The NHS says some people need a higher dose, for example those with diabetes or taking medicine for epilepsy, and that this is arranged with a doctor.

body.heading: Can too much be harmful?
body.body: For vitamin D, the NHS says there is an upper daily limit for vitamin D supplements above which they could be harmful, and this applies to adults, pregnant and breastfeeding women and children aged 11 to 17. For folic acid, the NHS says low supplement amounts are unlikely to cause harm, and that higher amounts can mask the symptoms of vitamin B12 deficiency.

body.heading: What do some common nutrients do?
body.body: For vitamin A, the NHS says most people should be able to get all they need from a varied and balanced diet. The NHS says vitamin D helps regulate the amount of calcium and phosphate in the body. It says that from about late March or early April to the end of September most people can make all the vitamin D they need from sunlight on the skin. Iron is important for making red blood cells, which carry oxygen around the body. Liver is very rich in vitamin A; the NHS says liver or liver products such as pâté should not be eaten more than once a week, and advises people who are pregnant to avoid them.
